title: National Lampoon'
full_review:
When his father cuts him off, a perennial college student supports himself by becoming the official campus party planner in the crude gross-out comedy "National Lampoon's Van Wilder" (Artisan).

This story is the Peter Pan syndrome reinterpreted in the National Lampoon series' style: gratuitous sex and nudity, lowbrow, scatological humor, and juvenile, disgusting situations that would find pastry chefs and PETA supporters in an unlikely alliance. Van Wilder (Ryan Reynolds, better known as Berg on TV's "Two Guys and A Girl") is what some might call an eternal senior, a guy who won't face reality, so instead he tries to stick around campus as long as he can. But when his fed-up father (Tim Matheson) refuses to pay for one more semester, Van finds a way to support himself. He decides to organize outlandish parties for the student body willing to pay him for his services.

The first of the National Lampoon series, 1978's "Animal House," shocked with its cavalier grossness, but at the very least (and this is a backhanded compliment if there ever was one), it was original. Uninspired and witless, "Van Wilder" churns out familiar gross-out jokes recycled from the other films of this sub-genre. Although Reynolds can be charming every once and a great while, he is surrounded by non-stop stupidity in the form of base humor and vile practical jokes. What is supposed to be the set piece of the film is a repulsive scene mixing a doggy emission, fake eclairs and their ingestion by unsuspecting characters. Can a film sink any lower?

Van is of course given a love interest: the no-nonsense Gwen (Tara Reid), a student journalist who eventually shows Van that he can be more than just the big man around campus. Their romance is forced and predictable, which just about sizes up director Walt Becker's film.

Save your money.

Because of a few sexual encounters, many coarse sexual references, exploitative nudity, some drug abuse, underage drinking and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
